q: The recruiter says the next step is "a technical round". What should you do first?
options: Spend the week on algorithm exercises, since every technical round is LeetCode-style
Ask the recruiter for the format of that round and of the rest of the loop
Assume it is system design, the round most senior loops include
Prepare every topic equally so that no format can surprise you
explain: Formats vary widely between Paris companies: live coding in TDD, a 2-hour test, a 3-day take-home with a review, a bug bash, a design round. Asking is normal and tells you what to prepare. Algorithm rounds remain at big tech and Datadog, but most loops grade other skills.

q: At the recruiter screen you are asked for your salary expectations for a senior backend role in Paris. Which answer is best?
options: "Whatever you think is fair for the role; I trust you to make a good offer."
"My current salary plus 10 percent, which is the usual step when changing jobs."
"From my research on Paris senior backend roles, X to Y gross annual fixed. What is your range?"
"A single precise figure slightly below the market, so that the company sees a safe hire and keeps me in."
explain: A researched range, stated as gross annual fixed, anchors the discussion on the market and the level of the role, and asking for the budget gives you information in return. A figure set low to stay in the process is hard to raise later, and "whatever is fair" lets the other side anchor.

q: Why does decideCancellation(order, now) take the current instant as a parameter?
options: So that tests can pass a fixed instant and never depend on the date they run on
Because Date.now() is not available when Node strips TypeScript types at startup
To make the function faster by avoiding a system call
Because node:test refuses tests that read the clock
explain: Passing now in makes the rule a pure function: the tests use a fixed PLACED_AT and minutes after it, so they give the same result on any day. Date.now() works fine under type stripping and node:test has no such rule; the reason is testability, not speed.

q: What does the line const unhandled: never = order.status; in the default branch give you?
options: It throws at runtime as soon as the function is called
It converts the status to a string for the error message
It makes the switch run faster by telling V8 the branch is unreachable
A compile error when a new status is added and not handled
explain: If every member of the union is handled, the type left in default is never and the assignment compiles. Adding 'refunded' without a case made TypeScript 6.0.3 report that it is not assignable to never. The line has no effect on speed, and it only throws if an unexpected value arrives at runtime.

q: What belongs in the "Trade-offs" section of a take-home README?
options: The list of libraries used, with their versions
Each design choice, what it costs, and when you would change it
An apology for each feature you did not have time to build, with the reason
The full specification copied from the brief
explain: The reviewers pick their questions from your trade-offs, so writing them as choice, cost and condition lets you choose the ground of the defence. Missing features belong in a factual "with one more day" list, not an apology; versions belong in the stack line.

q: In the code review round, in what order should you read and comment on the pull request?
options: Security and data integrity, then failure handling, then concurrency, then style
Naming and style first, since they are the quickest wins and set the tone of the review
Top to bottom, commenting each line in the order the author wrote it
Tests first, and the code itself only if the tests look incomplete or wrong
explain: Reading by risk makes sure the bugs that break production (an injection, a missing deadline, a race) are raised first, whatever time remains. Line-by-line reading spends the round on whatever comes first in the file, often style, and a passing happy-path test says little about those bugs.

q: In Conventional Comments, what does the decoration (blocking) on a comment mean?
options: The reviewer will block the author on the chat tool until it is fixed
The comment is a nitpick about formatting
The change should not be accepted until the comment is resolved
The comment can be ignored unless the change is minor
explain: The Conventional Comments page defines blocking as a comment that should prevent the change from being accepted until it is resolved. Skipping unless the change is minor is the meaning of (if-minor), and a nitpick is a label, not a decoration.

q: In a bug bash, a checkout test fails in a repo you have never seen. What is the first step of the method?
options: Read the whole codebase so that you understand it before touching anything
Rewrite the function the test calls, since it is probably wrong
Ask the interviewer where the bug is
Reproduce it by running only that test, then read the whole error
explain: Reproducing alone (with --test-name-pattern or vitest -t) gives a fast loop, and the full error (message, actual and expected values, first stack frame in the repo) usually points to the hypothesis. Reading the whole codebase wastes the round, and rewriting before understanding is the guessing the round grades against.

q: During git bisect run ./check.sh, the script exits with code 125 on one commit. What does git do?
options: It marks the commit as bad, like any non-zero exit code
It skips that commit as untestable and continues
It aborts the bisect, because 125 is outside the range for bad commits
It marks the commit as good and moves to the next midpoint
explain: The git documentation reserves 125 for "cannot be tested": the commit is skipped. Codes 1 to 127 other than 125 mean bad, 0 means good, and any other code (128 and above) aborts the bisect.

q: In a round where an AI assistant is allowed, what is the interviewer mainly grading?
options: How you direct the assistant and how you check what it produces
How fast the assistant produces working code compared with other candidates
Whether you finish the task without ever using the assistant
How short your prompts are
explain: In these rounds (Canva since 2025, Meta from October 2025) the candidate is judged on directing and checking the AI: precise context, reading every line, running the tests, deciding visibly. The speed of the tool is not your skill, and refusing the assistant misses what the round measures.

q: In a STAR answer, where should most of the time go?
options: The Situation, so that the interviewer understands the context fully
The Result, with as many numbers as possible
The Action: what you did yourself, said with "I"
The Task, to show how important your responsibility was
explain: The interviewer evaluates your behaviour, which lives in the actions you took, so they should be the core of a two-minute story, in the first person. A long situation is the common mistake: two sentences of context are enough.

q: At the end of the live coding round, which question to the engineer is the most useful?
options: "Did I pass this round, and how did I do compared with the others?"
"How many days of remote work per week does the team have?"
"Could you tell me what the company does, and who its main customers are?"
"What was your last production incident, and what changed after it?"
explain: An engineer can answer it from experience, and the answer tells you how incidents, on-call and follow-ups really work. Remote policy belongs to the recruiter, asking what the company does shows no preparation, and "Did I pass?" puts the interviewer in an awkward position without giving you information.

q: During live coding the interviewer says: "Prices are in euros, just use floating-point numbers." What is the best response?
options: Agree: JavaScript numbers are exact up to two decimal places, which is enough for prices
Propose integer cents, show why floats are inexact, then follow their choice
Refuse to continue until a decimal library is installed in the shared editor
Use floats, and round with toFixed(2) after every operation to keep amounts exact
explain: The line prints 0.30000000000000004 on Node 24: binary floats cannot represent most decimal fractions. Proposing integer cents, with the reason, shows judgement, and following the interviewer afterwards keeps the round moving. Rounding at every step hides the error and accumulates rounding decisions; refusing to continue is not collaboration.

q: You agreed that the 30th minute is included. Your tests so far cover 10 minutes after placement (accepted) and 45 minutes after (refused). Which test should you add next?
options: A test at 20 minutes, to have one more accepted case
A test that checks the error message text
A test at exactly 30 minutes and one at one millisecond after
A test that reads the real clock, to check it in real conditions
explain: Bugs sit at the boundary: > versus >= changes only the result at exactly 30 minutes, so that case and the instant just after it pin the rule. Another case at 20 minutes passes with either comparison, and a test that reads the real clock depends on when it runs.

q: The project runs with node src/server.ts on Node 24, and CI runs tsc --noEmit. A colleague adds 'refunded' to OrderStatus without a new case in decideCancellation, whose default branch assigns the status to never. What happens?
options: Node runs it, since it never checks types; the CI type check fails on the never line
Node refuses to start, with a type error on the never line
Both succeed: TypeScript widens never to include the new status
The CI type check passes, and the function throws only when a refunded order arrives in production
explain: Verified: the modified file ran under node with exit code 0, while TypeScript 6.0.3 reported "Type '"refunded"' is not assignable to type 'never'". Node only erases types and never checks them, which is why the type check must stay in CI. The runtime throw only happens if nobody ran the type check.

q: In the defence of your take-home, a reviewer points at this code: "Two customers buy the last unit at the same time. What happens?" What is the best answer?
options: Nothing bad happens: the UPDATE is atomic, so the second request waits for the first and then fails
Wrapping both queries in a transaction fixes it, because a transaction isolates the two requests
Only one can pass, because PostgreSQL locks the row during the SELECT
Both can see one unit and sell it; I would use one conditional UPDATE and check the row count
explain: A plain SELECT takes no row lock, so both requests can read one unit before either updates; the UPDATE is atomic but nothing re-checks the quantity. A transaction at the default Read Committed level lets the same race through (M09). The conditional UPDATE makes the check and the write one statement, and an affected row count of 0 means out of stock.

q: A take-home brief says "about 4 hours of work" and gives you 3 days. What should you deliver?
options: Everything you can build in 3 days, to stand out clearly from the other candidates in the pool
The core path done well in about 4 hours, with tests and a README naming what is left out
A minimal version with no tests, since tests were not mentioned
A full microservice architecture, to show senior design skills
explain: Respecting the expected effort shows you can scope, and the README turns omissions into decisions the reviewers can discuss. Three days of work makes the comparison unfair to read and gives the reviewers more surface to question; skipping tests or over-architecting both miss what the review checks.

q: The orders table holds three orders. What does this query return when orderId is x' OR '1'='1?
options: No row, because no order has that id
An error, because the quotes are unbalanced
All three orders, because the condition becomes always true
Only the first order, because a WHERE on id returns at most one row
explain: The SQL becomes WHERE id = 'x' OR '1'='1', which is true for every row: run on PostgreSQL 18.6, it returned all 3 orders, while the same value passed as $1 returned none. The quotes balance because the injected value closes and reopens them, which is exactly how injection works.

q: In the PR, the restock query has no await. One day that query fails with a deadlock error. With Node 24's default flags and no rejection handler, what happens?
options: It has already returned success; the rejection is unhandled and the process exits with code 1
The function waits for the query anyway, because every promise inside an async function is awaited
The error is silently ignored and the stock stays wrong
The caller's try/catch receives the deadlock error
explain: Without await, the function returns before the query settles, so the caller sees success and its try/catch never sees the error. Measured on Node 24: the handler returned, then the unhandled rejection crashed the process with exit code 1, taking the other in-flight requests with it. It is not ignored either: since Node 15 an unhandled rejection is raised as an uncaught exception.

q: Two cancel requests for order 1042 arrive at the same moment, on two replicas. The code reads the status, refunds if it is paid, then sets cancelled. Which fix would you ask for?
options: An in-memory Map of the order ids being cancelled, checked by the handler before the refund
A 500 ms delay before the refund, so the first request has time to finish its update
A unique index on orders.status, so two rows cannot change state together
A conditional UPDATE … WHERE status = 'paid' RETURNING, and a refund only if a row comes back
explain: The conditional UPDATE makes the database decide which request wins: in a scratch run, two concurrent check-then-act calls refunded twice, and the conditional UPDATE refunded once. An in-memory Map only protects one process, and here the requests are on two replicas; a delay only narrows the window.

q: Which review comment on the injection bug is best?
options: "This is wrong, please fix it before I look at the rest of the pull request."
"issue (blocking): orderId is concatenated into the SQL, so callers can inject SQL. Pass it as $1."
"nitpick (non-blocking): maybe use a parameter here instead of building the SQL string by hand?"
"Why would anyone write SQL like this in 2026? We have had parameters for years."
explain: It states the problem, its severity, the evidence and the fix, in the Conventional Comments format. Labelling a security bug as a nitpick tells the author it is optional, which is the opposite of the truth, and the other two comments give no reason and no way forward.

q: You ask for AbortSignal.timeout(3_000) on the refund call and a retry when it times out. What else must the retry have?
options: A longer timeout on each new attempt, so that the last attempt always has time to succeed
Nothing: a call that timed out never reached the provider
The same idempotency key on every attempt, so the provider refunds only once
A new payment id for each attempt, so the provider does not reject duplicates
explain: A timeout only tells you that you stopped waiting: the provider may have processed the first refund. Sending the same idempotency key on every attempt lets it recognise the retry and answer with the first result (M02). A new id per attempt is precisely how a customer gets refunded twice.

q: This integration test against PostgreSQL fails with '4500499' !== 4999. What is the cause?
options: sum() is a bigint, which node-postgres returns as a string, so + concatenates
The cart has a second line priced 499 cents that the test fixture forgot to remove
TypeScript compiled + as string concatenation because of the generic type on query
PostgreSQL returned the sum in euros, not in cents
explain: On PostgreSQL 18.6, pg_typeof of the sum is bigint, and the pg-types README states that node-postgres returns int8 results as strings. '4500' + 499 is '4500499'. TypeScript emits no code for +: the generic on query is an unchecked assertion, so the type said number while the value was a string.

q: A test of the export "orders sorted by total" fails. What does this line print?
explain: Without a comparator, sort converts the values to strings and compares them in UTF-16 order, so "999" comes after "4500" (verified on Node 24). Pass a comparator: toSorted((a, b) => a - b) printed [ 999, 1200, 4500 ] and leaves the original array untouched.

q: paymentStatus() takes about 300 ms and deliveryEta() about 600 ms; neither needs the other's result. How long does this handler take, and what is the fix?
options: About 600 ms already, because Node starts the awaits in parallel by default
About 900 ms; with Promise.all over the two calls it drops to about 600 ms
About 900 ms, and nothing can be done without worker threads
About 300 ms, because the second await starts while the first one is still pending
explain: Each await waits before the next call starts, so the times add up: measured on Node 24 with timers, 911 ms sequentially and 604 ms with Promise.all, which starts both calls and waits for the slower. Waiting on I/O needs no worker thread.

q: In the bug bash, only GET /orders/:id is slow. The trace shows 850 ms in one SQL span; other routes and the event loop metrics are normal. What do you do next?
options: Add replicas of the API
Take a CPU profile of the Node process
Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on that query and read its plan
Add a cache in front of the route before investigating further
explain: The measurement already points at one query, so the next step is its plan, which shows a sequential scan or a bad join (M08). A CPU profile is the tool when every route is slow and the event loop is busy (M01), which is not the case; a cache or replicas hide the cause without finding it.

q: The assistant wrote this to retry a refund that times out. On Node 24, what happens when the 3-second deadline fires?
options: It is a TimeoutError, so the branch is skipped and the error is rethrown
The error is named AbortError, like any aborted signal, so the retry is scheduled
fetch resolves with a 408 response, so the catch block never runs
The error is a plain Error with code ETIMEDOUT, so the branch is skipped
explain: Measured against a slow local server: fetch rejected with a DOMException whose name is TimeoutError. AbortError is the name for a manual controller.abort(), which is why this check looks plausible. The fix tests for TimeoutError, with a test that simulates a slow provider.

q: The VP asks: "How has AI changed the way you build, and where do you not trust it?" Which answer is strongest?
options: "I do not use AI tools at all: I prefer to understand every line I write, and it keeps my skills sharp."
"It writes most of my code now, which makes me much faster than before; I mainly review the pull requests it opens."
"AI is overhyped for backend work, so I avoid relying on it except for writing documentation."
"Boilerplate and first drafts; I check every diff with tests and docs, and distrust it on concurrency and security."
explain: It is specific about what is delegated, how it is checked and where trust stops; in the round itself, add one real bug you caught as evidence. In the market check, 23% of Paris postings expect daily use of AI coding tools, so refusing them reads as a gap, and "it writes most of my code" without a checking method is what interviewers worry about.

q: The CEO asks you in one sentence: "Make checkout faster." What do you do before writing any code?
options: Start optimising the slowest SQL query you already know of in the checkout
Add a cache in front of the checkout so that the CEO sees quick results
Ask what "faster" means, measure the baseline, and agree on a target
Plan a rewrite of the checkout in a faster framework such as Fastify
explain: "Faster" can mean server latency, page load, fewer steps or higher conversion, and each leads to different work. Clarifying the goal, measuring the baseline and agreeing on success is what the question is designed to hear. Starting with the query you already know solves a problem nobody has confirmed.

q: With 10 minutes left in live coding, you realise your design cannot handle a requirement the interviewer just added. What do you do?
options: Keep typing silently and try to finish the original design before the time runs out completely
Say it, explain the change you would make, and finish the key part with tests green
Start a full rewrite from scratch, since a wrong design is worse than none
Argue that the new requirement is out of scope for a 90-minute exercise
explain: Naming the problem, the fix and its cost, then prioritising, shows exactly the judgement the round grades, and green tests keep what works safe. A rewrite in 10 minutes usually leaves nothing working, and silent typing hides the very reasoning the interviewer wants to hear.
